Unit 2:
World of
Color
Read Aloud
Dog’s Colorful Day: A Messy Story
about Colors and Counting
Big Ideas
Color is a property of many natural and human-made things.
We can all communicate about colors.
Guiding
Questions
How can we explore and communicate ideas and feelings through colors?
How do colors provide information?
Text to
Centers
Connections
Art Studio: Mixing Primary Colors
Library and Listening: Storytelling with Props
Family
Engagement
Ask families and caregivers to share humorous stories about getting dirty and
washing up (e.g., one time our baby sister spilled cheerios all over the
floor…). Share these connections during the reads.
Vocabulary
coat: a covering for an animal's body, such as fur on a dog
colorful: many colors
pollen: yellow powder found in flowers
race: to run
smear: a spot or mark made by spreading something on something else
stain: a mark that is hard to wash off

lessonRead1:
WEEK 4
Dog’s Colorful Day
Read 1 of 2: Introduce the book
Objectives
I am learning to:
●
Respond to questions about a read aloud text. (RL.PK.1.)
●
Become more familiar with new words in a story to better
understand the sequence of events. (RL.PK.4.)
●
"read" the illustrations in a picture book. (RL.PK.6.)
Before reading
Activate background knowledge and make connections to prior learning.
We’ve read so many books about colors, such as Mouse Paint and
Green is a Chile Pepper/Red is a Dragon! Colors give us important
information.
Introduce the text.
We have a new story to read today, the title of this book is Dog’s
Colorful Day: A Messy Story about Colors and Counting. The author
and illustrator of this book is Emma Dodd.
Point to Dog.
Here is a picture of Dog. Hafis fur coat is all white, except for one
black spot on his ear. Dog spends the day playing and exploring, and
he gets dirty!
Set a purpose for reading.
Let’s read the story and find out what type of spots Dog gets on his
fur and why he has a colorful day.
While reading
pages 3-4
Read the full text, cover to cover. As the story proceeds, invite children to
chime in with counting the spots or predicting the number of spots.
Jam is similar to jelly. Put your hand on your head if you like peanut
butter and jelly sandwiches!
Look at that jam that drips on his back.
pages 7-8
Before reading the page, ask children to “read the illustration”.
What do you think will happen? How do you know?
Prompt children to describe what they see in the illustration.

You are correct! Dog’s coat, or covering on his body, is white. And
now it’s covered in a green stain of grass. A stain is something that
is hard to wash off.
pages 11-12
Pollen is a yellow powder from the center of flowers that bees carry
from flower to flower.
pages 13-14
Before reading the page, ask children to “read the illustration”.
What do you think will happen? How do you know?
Prompt children to describe what they see in the illustration.
Yes! Dog trots, or walks quickly, through the park, and ice cream
lands on his ear!
pages 19-20
Dog races inside the house, or runs in.
Show how you might run in place.
pages 21-22
Let’s count Dog’s colorful spots together. Colorful means there are
many colors.
Point to the spots on Dog while counting.
pages 23-24
A smear of chocolate is a spot made by spreading chocolate.
Before turning the page, ask children for a prediction.
What should Vicky do to help Dog?
After reading
Show page 29.
How has Dog had a colorful day?
How can you have a colorful day?
Closing
Today we read Dog’s Colorful Day. We made predictions and also
talked about why he had a colorful day.
Standards
RL.PK.1. With prompting and support, ask and answer questions about a
story or poem read aloud.
RL.PK.4. With prompting and support, ask and answer questions about
unfamiliar words in a story or poem read aloud.
RL.PK.6. With prompting and support, "read" the illustrations in a picture
book by describing a character or place depicted or by telling how a
sequence of events unfolds.
Ongoing
assessment
Listen to children’s responses during the read and also after.
●
How are they responding to the questions?
●
How do the children show their understanding of new words?
●
How are they explaining their predictions and their thinking for
these predictions?
